summary: Specifies the Host Identity Protocol, which lets hosts securely set up IP-layer state and separates the identity of a host from its address. This keeps communication going when addresses change. It uses a Diffie-Hellman exchange with public key identifiers and resists denial-of-service and man-in-the-middle attacks. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 7401.

plainLanguage.summary: Your name stays the same even when you move house. HIP lets computers keep a lasting identity so conversations survive address changes.

subtitle: Separating host identity from IP address to survive address changes and provide strong authentication.

tldr.problem: IP addresses serve two incompatible roles: they are routing locators (where packets are sent) and host identifiers (who endpoints are). When an address changes, connections break, and there is no strong authentication at the IP layer.
tldr.mechanism: HIP introduces a new namespace using public cryptographic keys as Host Identifiers (with short 128-bit representations called Host Identity Tags). A four-packet authenticated Diffie-Hellman base exchange establishes secure state between hosts before data flows, with a puzzle mechanism protecting against denial-of-service attacks.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can maintain secure associations and change addresses without breaking established connections. The protocol was experimental and was replaced by RFC 7401, which provides an updated version.

today: RFC 5201 defines the Host Identity Protocol as an Experimental protocol. It was superseded by RFC 7401, which provides an updated version. Related mobility and multihoming extensions are defined in RFC 5206, DNS integration in RFC 5205, and ESP transport format usage in RFC 5202.

sections.title: The Identity and Locator Problem
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol solves a fundamental problem with IP addressing: addresses are used for two incompatible purposes. Locators are routing labels identifying where a packet should be sent in the network. Identifiers are names for endpoints that upper layer protocols bind to. When an IP address changes due to mobility or multihoming, existing connections break because the locator has changed, even though the endpoint's identity has not.

HIP introduces a new namespace using public cryptographic keys as Host Identifiers. Upper layer protocols bind to this stable identity, while IP addresses become purely locators. The protocol enables dynamic IP address changes, provides strong mutual authentication at the IP layer, and resists denial-of-service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it like your name versus your address. Your name doesn't change when you move, but your address does. Normally, the phone system uses your address to find you, so changing address breaks your phone calls. HIP uses your name instead, so calls still work when you move.

sections.title: Host Identifiers and Identity Tags
sections.content:
In HIP, a host's identity is its public key from an asymmetric key pair (the private key stays with the host). The RFC requires support for RSA/SHA1 and recommends DSA; other algorithms may be supported. Because public keys are variable length and unsuitable for use in packet headers, HIP uses Host Identity Tags (HITs): 128-bit hashes of the Host Identifier.

The HIT is self-certifying, meaning it is computationally hard to find a Host Identifier that matches a given HIT. A HIT is the same length as an IPv6 address and can fit in standard address-sized fields in protocols and APIs. Both the Initiator's and Responder's HITs are carried in HIP packets to identify the endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: The Host Identifier is like your passport (proving who you are), but it's too long to carry everywhere. The Host Identity Tag is a short fingerprint of your passport. Computers include both HITs in their messages so they know who they're talking to.

sections.title: The Base Exchange and Four-Packet Handshake
sections.content:
The HIP base exchange is a four-packet authenticated Diffie-Hellman key exchange. The Initiator sends a trigger packet (I1) containing its HIT and optionally the Responder's HIT. The Responder sends R1, which includes a cryptographic puzzle, initial Diffie-Hellman parameters, its public key, and a signature over parts of the message.

The Initiator then solves the puzzle and sends I2, containing the puzzle solution, its Diffie-Hellman parameters, its (optionally encrypted) Host Identifier, and a signature. Finally, the Responder sends R2, a signed completion packet. Once R2 is received and verified, the HIP association is established and can be used with protocols like ESP for data integrity and encryption.

The puzzle mechanism protects the Responder from denial-of-service attacks: the Responder can remain stateless and pre-calculate R1 packets, dropping spoofed I2 packets cheaply by verifying the puzzle solution using the Initiator's HIT.
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake is like proving your identity before making a secure phone call. First, you say hello. The other person sends back a riddle to prove you're not a spam bot. You solve it and send your passport. They verify it and send back a confirmation. Now you can talk securely.

sections.title: Association States and Data Transfer
sections.content:
HIP defines several states during the exchange: UNASSOCIATED (initial), I1-SENT (Initiator waiting for R1), I2-SENT (Initiator waiting for R2), R2-SENT (Responder waiting for acknowledgment), ESTABLISHED (association active), CLOSING, CLOSED, and E-FAILED (exchange failed). Once established, a HIP association is bidirectional: either party can initiate future exchanges.

For actual data transfer, HIP uses Encapsulated Security Payload (ESP), a separate protocol defined in RFC 5202. HIP packets themselves are large (starting at 40 bytes), so the design compresses headers: HIP packets only carry the base exchange and state updates, while data flows through ESP. The HIP packet header can be omitted from data packets entirely in some implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: After the handshake completes, the connection moves to ESTABLISHED state. To actually send data, they use a different, smaller packet format. The big HIP handshake messages are just for setup.

sections.title: Security and Denial-of-Service Protection
sections.content:
HIP is designed to resist several attacks. The puzzle mechanism prevents the Responder from storing state per Initiator until a valid I2 (containing the puzzle solution) is received. An attacker cannot generate spoofed I2 packets across multiple different HITs without solving a puzzle for each one, because the puzzle is based on the Initiator's HIT.

Mutual authentication occurs via signature verification: the Initiator verifies the Responder's signature on R1, and both parties verify each other's signatures on I2 and R2. The protocol generates session keys from Diffie-Hellman shared secrets, which are kept secret from eavesdroppers. The design is based on the Sigma protocol, a proven secure model for authenticated key exchange.

The IESG notes in the RFC acknowledge limitations: the specification uses RSA, HMAC, and SHA-1 by default, which may not reflect current best practices, and future versions should define more flexible cryptographic negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The hard-to-solve puzzle stops spam and attackers from flooding you with fake connection attempts. When you prove your identity with a signature, you prove you really have the private key. The shared secret they agree on is hidden even if someone watches all the messages.

sections.title: Mobility, Multihoming, and Updates
sections.content:
Once a HIP association is established, it can be updated without tearing down and re-establishing. UPDATE packets allow hosts to change IP addresses while keeping the same Host Identity and security association. This enables seamless mobility: a host can move to a new network, change its IP address, and send an UPDATE packet to signal the new address. Since the communication is keyed to the Host Identity Tag, not the IP address, the connection survives.

Multihoming is similarly supported: a single host can have multiple IP addresses and maintain a single HIP association with multiple address pairs. Related specifications (RFC 5206 for mobility and multihoming, RFC 5204 for rendezvous) extend HIP with mechanisms for hosts to be reached at new addresses even when their current IP is unknown.
sections.plainLanguage: After the connection is set up, you can move to a new IP address and tell the other side where you are now. They keep the same encrypted connection even though your address changed. You can also have multiple addresses at the same time.
